pass that constant down from the place where it makes sense to know it to
the place that actually uses it.

Conceptual Affinity. Certain bits of code want to be near other bits. They
have a certain conceptual affinity. The stronger that affinity, the less vertical
distance there should be between them.

As we have seen, this affinity might be based on a direct dependence, such
as one function calling another, or a function using a variable. But there are
other possible causes of affinity. Affinity might be caused because a group
of functions perform a similar operation. Consider this snippet of code from
Junit 4.3.1:



   public class Assert {
     static public void assertTrue(String message, boolean condition) {
       if (!condition)
         fail(message);
     }

     static public void assertTrue(boolean condition) {
       assertTrue(null, condition);
     }

     static public void assertFalse(String message, boolean condition) {
       assertTrue(message, !condition);
     }

     static public void assertFalse(boolean condition) {
       assertFalse(null, condition);
     }
   …

These functions have a strong conceptual affinity because they share a
common naming scheme and perform variations of the same basic task. The
fact that they call each other is secondary. Even if they didn’t, they would
still want to be close together.

Vertical Ordering

In general we want function call dependencies to point in the downward
direction. That is, a function that is called should be below a function that
does the calling.2 This creates a nice flow down the source code module
from high level to low level.
2. This is the exact opposite of languages like Pascal, C, and C++ that enforce functions to be
defined, or at least declared, before they are used.

As in newspaper articles, we expect the most important concepts to come
first, and we expect them to be expressed with the least amount of polluting
detail. We expect the low-level details to come last. This allows us to skim
source files, getting the gist from the first few functions, without having to
immerse ourselves in the details. Listing 5-5 is organized this way. Perhaps
even better examples are Listing 15-5 on page 263, and Listing 3-7 on page
50.



Horizontal Formatting

How wide should a line be? To answer that, let’s look at how wide lines are
in typical programs. Again, we examine the seven different projects. Figure
5-2 shows the distribution of line lengths of all seven projects. The
regularity is impressive, especially right around 45 characters. Indeed,
every size from 20 to 60 represents about 1 percent of the total number of
lines. That’s 40 percent! Perhaps another 30 percent are less than 10
characters wide. Remember this is a log scale, so the linear appearance of
the drop-off above 80 characters is really very significant. Programmers
clearly prefer short lines.

Figure 5-2 Java line width distribution

This suggests that we should strive to keep our lines short. The old
Hollerith limit of 80 is a bit arbitrary, and I’m not opposed to lines edging
out to 100 or even 120. But beyond that is probably just careless.

I used to follow the rule that you should never have to scroll to the right.
But monitors are too wide for that nowadays, and younger programmers
can shrink the font so small that they can get 200 characters across the
screen. Don’t do that. I personally set my limit at 120.



Horizontal Openness and Density

We use horizontal white space to associate things that are strongly related
and disassociate things that are more weakly related. Consider the following
function:
   private void measureLine(String line) {
     lineCount++;
     int lineSize = line.length();
     totalChars += lineSize;

I surrounded the assignment operators with white space to accentuate them.
Assignment statements have two distinct and major elements: the left side
and the right side. The spaces make that separation obvious.

On the other hand, I didn’t put spaces between the function names and the
opening parenthesis. This is because the function and its arguments are
closely related. Separating them makes them appear disjoined instead of
conjoined. I separate arguments within the function call parenthesis to
accentuate the comma and show that the arguments are separate.

Another use for white space is to accentuate the precedence of operators.
   public class Quadratic {
     public static double root1(double a, double b, double c) {
       double determinant = determinant(a, b, c);
       return (-b + Math.sqrt(determinant)) / (2*a);
     }

     public static double root2(int a, int b, int c) {
       double determinant = determinant(a, b, c);
       return (-b - Math.sqrt(determinant)) / (2*a); 
     }

     private static double determinant(double a, double b, double c) {
       return b*b - 4*a*c;
     }
   }

Notice how nicely the equations read. The factors have no white space
between them because they are high precedence. The terms are separated by
white space because addition and subtraction are lower precedence.

Unfortunately, most tools for reformatting code are blind to the precedence
of operators and impose the same spacing throughout. So subtle spacings
like those shown above tend to get lost after you reformat the code.

For a **120,000-watt inverter**, the shore power feed is determined by:

\[
I = \frac{P}{V}
\]

Where:  
- \(P = 120{,}000 \, \text{W}\) (inverter capacity)  
- \(V\) = input shore voltage (120V single-phase, 240V split-phase, or 480V three-phase depending on setup)

---

### Typical Scenarios
1. **120V single-phase**  
   \[
   I = \frac{120{,}000}{120} = 1{,}000 \, \text{A}
   \]  
   → Requires massive bussing and multiple paralleled breakers. Not practical.

2. **240V split-phase (common in residential/light commercial)**  
   \[
   I = \frac{120{,}000}{240} \approx 500 \, \text{A}
   \]  
   → You’d be looking at **a 500A service breaker** (or parallel 250A–400A breakers feeding separate legs).

3. **480V three-phase (common in industrial/commercial)**  
   \[
   I = \frac{120{,}000}{\sqrt{3} \cdot 480} \approx 144 \, \text{A}
   \]  
   → A **150A three-pole breaker** is typical here.

---

### What This Means for Your Shore Feed
- If you’re wiring this into a **residential barn/shop in Howell, MI** with standard **240V service**, you’ll need at least a **500A breaker** (and service conductors sized accordingly, typically 600 kcmil copper or larger).  
- If you have the option of **480V three-phase service** (not common for residential, but possible in commercial/agricultural setups), you’d only need about a **150A breaker**, which is far more manageable.  

---

⚡ **Important:**  
- NEC requires derating for continuous loads (usually 125%), so actual breaker size may need to be larger.  
- Wire sizing, breaker choice, and disconnects should all be engineered with an electrician — at **120kW, you’re in utility-grade equipment territory**, not typical residential panels.  

---

Got it—no math, just real-world specs. I looked into typical three-phase inverter systems around the 120 kW range to see what kind of input (shore/grid-side) amperage they’re built for. Here’s what manufacturers are specifying:

---

###  CSI Solar (75–120 kW String Inverter)
Two configurations:
- **12-input model (6 MPPTs)**: **Max AC output current ≈ 182.3 A** citeturn1search0turn1search20  
- **18-input model (9 MPPTs)**: similarly rated citeturn1search20  

So, you'd generally plan for **around 180 A per phase** on the AC input (shore power side).

---

###  SolaX X3 FORTH PLUS (120 kW)
From the technical spec sheet, the inverter’s output parameters (but typical rating is in line with similar numbers, though they don’t list the exact output current) citeturn1search1.

---

###  SolarEdge Synergy 120 kW (277/480 VAC)
Output spec:
- **Max continuous output current at 208 V per phase**: **145 A** citeturn0search11turn1search5  

At 480 VAC, current would be lower (but spec isn’t listed). Still, at 208 V per phase it's 145 A, reinforcing the 150–200 A per-phase ballpark.

---

###  GoodWe HT Series (up to 120 kW)
While the inverter spec doesn’t show output current directly, it indicates **max DC input current per string: 15 A** citeturn1search13turn1search16. That helps on the DC side but not the shore AC feed.

---

###  Summary Table

| Inverter Model / Brand         | AC Input (Shore/Grid) Current (Per Phase) |
|--------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| CSI 75–120 kW                  | ~182 A                                     |
| SolarEdge Synergy (208 V)      | ~145 A                                     |
| SolaX X3 FORTH PLUS (120 kW)   | Comparable — around 150–200 A               |
| GoodWe HT Series (120 kW)      | Unspecified, likely similar range           |

---

###  Bottom Line
For most **120 kW three-phase grid-tie or shore-fed inverters**, the typical **AC input current per phase is between 145 A and 185 A**. In practical terms, that means breaker sizes of **150–200 A per phase** are standard for shore power feeding these systems.

---

- **30A panel** is holding up fine.

  - Kitchen (minus heavy loads simultaneously)
  - Computer
  - Furnace
  - Lighting
  - Well pump
- No breaker trips → you're likely pulling **well under 30 amps continuous**, even with spikes.

---

### What This Tells Us
You're in a **light to moderate usage** profile — perfect for staged solar integration. A few key points:

#### ✅ Your baseline usage proves:
- You **don’t need 120,000 W (120 kW)** of inverter to support normal operations unless you’re planning for:
  - Full off-grid with HVAC and shop tools
  - EV charging
  - Large-scale battery storage
  - Feeding multiple buildings

#### 🛠 If your future goal is to scale up:
- You could:
  - Start with a **10–30 kW system** (matching current breaker limits)
  - Use your **30A panel as a subpanel** off the inverter for protected loads
  - Add **load shedding** or **smart control** to avoid overloads
  - Go hybrid: grid + solar + battery, and slowly scale toward 120 kW as budget/needs grow

Great, thanks for clarifying! You're looking at a **10 kW, 48 V split‑phase inverter/charger** like the SunGoldPower SPH10K48SP. Let’s check typical shore‑power (AC input) current specs for that unit:

---

###  SunGoldPower 10 kW Split‑Phase Inverter — AC Input Insights

From the spec sheet, this inverter features a built-in AC charger with these characteristics:  
- **Max mains/generator (AC) charging current**: **120 A** citeturn0search12turn0search8.

That means, when feeding off shore power (or generator), it can draw up to **120 A** from the AC source to recharge batteries or support loads. If you're powering the inverter from a shore feed directly, you’d need wiring and a breaker sized accordingly.

---

###  Technical Breakdown:
- **Output side**: Delivers 10 kW at 120/240 V split phase, meaning up to ~41.7 A per 240 V leg—but that's output, not what the inverter draws from shore power citeturn0search18turn0search17.
- **AC input side**: The key figure is that charger capability—**120 A input** from generator or grid citeturn0search12turn0search8.

---

###  What Does This Mean for Your 30 A Panel?
Your current generator panel is rated at **30 A**, which works fine for your existing load (kitchen, lighting, well, etc.) because you're not using full inverter charging.

However, if you plan to have the inverter actively **charging batteries or handling heavy loads via shore power**, the system could attempt to draw **up to 120 A**, which would overload your current setup.

---

###  Summary Table

| Function                         | Approx. Shore Power Input |
|----------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Regular inverter output load     | < Current panel can handle |
| Active charging or heavy loads   | **Up to 120 A — panel would overload** |

---

###  Recommendation
If you're planning to operate the inverter in hybrid mode—meaning it uses shore power to charge batteries or support high loads—you’ll need to upgrade your shore feed:

- A service breaker rated **around 120 A** (plus margin).
- Proper wire gauge and subpanel setup to safely support that current.

You might consider integrating the inverter into your main panel or setting up a transfer switch to handle switching between shore power and solar/battery sources safely.

You're spot on—and yes, a **PEX solar thermal box absolutely can work**, *if designed right*. With your space, spare tank, and plumbing skills, you’re 90% there already.

---

### ✅ Key Design Principle:
**Solar hot water is not about hitting 212°F—it’s about slow, steady heat gain.**  
PEX can absolutely transfer enough heat into water, especially with a smart layout and proper thermal trapping.

---

### 🔧 Here's How to Make It Work:

#### 🧵 1. **PEX Thermal Box Basics**
- Use **black PEX** (absorbs more heat) or paint it black with high-temp matte
- Mount inside a box:
  - **Insulated bottom**
  - **Clear polycarbonate/glass top** (acts like a greenhouse)
  - Sloped for **optimal sun angle** (usually ≈ your latitude)
- **Coil or serpentine layout** for PEX
  - Tighter spacing = better heat transfer
- Reflective inner surfaces help bounce light back into PEX

#### 🧵 2. **Water Loop Design**
- Use **closed-loop glycol** or direct water:
  - Closed loop with a **heat exchanger** is safer in freezing climates
  - Direct-loop is simpler and cheaper (but can freeze)
- Push with **DC pump (solar powered)** or a temp-triggered circulation loop

#### 🧵 3. **Integration with Tank**
- Reuse your **50-gal tank** as a **solar preheat tank**
- Replace heating elements with:
  - **Temp probes**
  - Optional **aux heating element** on a smart relay (backup heat)
- Plumbing:
  - Cold in → solar preheat tank → existing hot water tank (optional)
  - OR direct to outlets if pressure/temp is adequate

---

### 🔥 Temperature Expectations
On a sunny day with well-insulated box:
- **PEX internal water temps** can reach **130–150°F+** inside the box
- **Tank temps** of 90–120°F are very realistic
- In summer, you’ll probably need a thermal bypass to prevent boiling
- In winter, it will still preheat from 40°F to 80–100°F — that’s a big energy saver

---

### 🧠 Pro Tips
- Add **phase-change material (PCM)** or even dark thermal mass (like black bricks or steel plates) to **buffer and retain heat**
- Put your **temp sensors on PEX return + tank mid-point**
- Use **insulated PEX** between panel and tank to avoid thermal losses
- You can even experiment with **multi-box chaining** if you want to scale

---

### 📏 Rule of Thumb
1 ft² of collector surface = ~1–1.5 gallons of usable hot water per day  
So, a 4×8' box = 32 ft² = **30–45 gallons/day preheated**

---

### 🛠 If You Want to Start Simple
- Build one 4×8' insulated box
- Lay ~100–150' of 1/2" or 3/4" black PEX in a serpentine
- Add clear cover + foam insulation base
- Run cold water through it manually into a barrel
- Check temps on sunny days — you’ll likely hit 100–140°F by midafternoon

---

You’re asking exactly the right question — this is **the core plumbing challenge** of DIY solar thermal:  
🧠 **How do you circulate water in a loop that’s under pressure without triggering the well pump or fighting backpressure?**

---

### ✅ You’re right on all counts:
- A **pressurized loop** connected to the well system **will trigger the pump** if water flows out
- You **can’t just loop water through the tank’s lower and upper ports** unless it’s isolated from household pressure
- Without a **heat exchanger**, you'd either have to:
  - Dump pressure (and waste water), or
  - **Isolate the loop** as a **closed system** with its own fluid

---

## 💡 Solution: Use a Closed Loop + Heat Exchanger

### 🔁 Closed Loop = Self-contained fluid loop
- **No connection to household pressure**
- Circulates **glycol or water** in a PEX loop
- Heats the water in the tank via **thermal conduction**

---

### 🧊 Heat Exchanger: What It Does
A **heat exchanger** transfers heat from the hot glycol/water in the solar loop **into your tank water** — without mixing the two fluids.

### 🧰 Options for DIY Heat Exchanger

#### 🔩 1. **Copper Coil Inside the Tank** (DIY & cheap)
- Wrap **20–50 feet of soft copper tubing** into a coil
- Insert into the **50-gal tank**
- Hook the coil ends to your solar loop
- Circulate water/glycol through the copper → **heats the tank’s water**
- ✅ Cheap, works well
- ⚠️ Must be **rated for potable contact** if in your active water tank (not just the solar loop)

#### 🔩 2. **External Plate Heat Exchanger** (store-bought)
- Used in radiant heating, breweries, etc.
- Fast, compact, efficient
- 💰 ~$60–150 (eBay, Amazon, or surplus HVAC supply)

#### 🔩 3. **Copper Pipe-on-Pipe** (DIY hybrid)
- Wrap copper pipe carrying hot fluid **around** a section of cold pipe
- Insulate the whole section
- Not as efficient, but works if built with enough surface area

---

### ✅ Now Your Solar Loop Looks Like:

```plaintext
[Closed solar loop w/ PEX] —> Pump —> PEX box (gets hot) —> Heat exchanger (in tank) —> back to loop
```

And **house water stays separate**, pressurized, and clean.

---

### 🔥 Pro Tips for Pumping in a Closed Loop
- Use a **12V or 24V DC pump** (solar panel powered if you like)
- Add a **temperature differential controller** (or DIY relay) to trigger only when PEX box is hotter than tank
- Include a **pressure relief valve + expansion tank** in the loop for safety

---

### 🧪 Bonus DIY Hack: Thermosiphon
If your PEX box is **above** the tank:
- You can **skip the pump entirely**
- Hot water rises, cold falls → self-circulating loop
- This only works if:
  - Solar collector is elevated
  - Pipes are short and large-diameter (1/2"+)

---

### Summary

| Option         | Cost | Buildable? | Efficient? | Notes |
|----------------|------|------------|------------|-------|
| Copper coil    | Low  | ✅ DIY      | ✅ Good     | Most common DIY method |
| Plate exchanger| Med  | ⚠️ Buy      | ✅✅ Very    | Needs circulation pump |
| Pipe-on-pipe   | Low  | ✅ Hackable | ⚠️ Low-Med  | Use only if desperate |
| No exchanger   | --   | ❌         | ❌          | Will cause pressure/flooding issues |

---

Perfect — a **sealed 50-gallon tank** is exactly what you want for building a **closed-loop solar preheat system** with an internal heat exchanger. Here's how to leverage that fully.

---

## ✅ Your Scenario Recap:
- **50-gal sealed tank**: not pressurized by well, not connected to household plumbing
- **30-gal electric tank**: active household water heater
- Goal: preheat incoming water using **solar + thermal loop**, without affecting water pressure or wasting energy

---

## 🧠 Here's the Clean Solution:  
**Use the 50-gal sealed tank as a passive thermal battery**  
**Add a DIY copper coil heat exchanger inside it**

### 🔁 System Flow

```plaintext
[Cold well water]
     ↓
[Coil heat exchanger inside 50-gal tank]
     ↓
[30-gal electric tank]
     ↓
[House faucets]
```

### 🔥 Solar Side (Closed Loop)
```plaintext
Pump → PEX solar box → 50-gal tank (heats water inside) → back to pump
```

So the **solar loop heats the water in the 50-gal tank**, and **your cold water flows through the internal coil**, picking up that heat on its way to the 30-gal tank.

---

## 🛠️ How to Build the Heat Exchanger

### Materials:
- 3/8" or 1/2" **soft copper tubing** (25–50 feet)
- NPT bulkhead fittings (for in/out ports)
- High-temp thread sealant
- Optional: silicone caulk + pipe insulation

### Steps:
1. **Coil the copper** into a spiral tight enough to fit through the top hole of the tank.
2. Feed it through the **element hole or port** on the 50-gal tank (usually 1" NPT).
3. Use **bulkhead fittings** to mount the coil ends through the wall (or top) of the tank.
4. Connect your **cold water inlet line** to one end of the coil.
5. Run the other coil end to your **30-gal tank’s inlet**.
6. Fill the 50-gal tank with clean water and seal it — it's now a sealed **thermal mass**.
7. Optional: Add a **temp sensor** port and insulation wrap to the whole tank.

---

## 💡 Why This Works So Well

- The solar loop runs on its own — no connection to house pressure
- You’re **not pumping potable water**, just transferring heat
- The sealed tank keeps heat for hours, even overnight
- You get **free water preheating** with zero pressure issues
- The 30-gal tank only “tops off” the temp if needed

---

## Bonus Option: Reuse the Upper Element Hole
- You could install a **backup 12V or 120V low-watt heater** as a fail-safe
- Or insert a **smart thermal sensor relay** to log water temps
- Just make sure it stays isolated from house pressure

---

## ✅ Option 1: **External Wrap Heat Exchanger** (DIY & Effective)

Instead of putting a coil **inside** the sealed tank, you:
- Wrap **soft copper tubing** **tightly around the outside** of the 50-gal tank
- Insulate the whole thing well (like a sleeping bag of foam wrap)

### 🔧 How to Do It:
1. Use **25–50 feet of 1/2" soft copper tubing**
2. Wrap it tightly around the **lower 2/3 of the tank** (where most heat stores)
3. Secure with metal strapping or high-temp tape
4. Wrap tank + coil in **R-10 or better insulation**
5. Connect the copper loop to your **cold water line in → out to 30-gal tank**

> 💡 The better your thermal contact and insulation, the more efficient this gets.  
> You can also put **heat-conductive paste or foil** between the copper and tank wall for better transfer.

---

## ✅ Option 2: Use the Tank’s **Existing Ports** as Entry Points

If your tank has:
- A **drain valve**
- Upper/lower **element ports**
- Or a **TPR valve port**

...you can **remove those** and install:
- A **short copper coil** through them (if large enough)
- Or **insert copper stubs** that act as a **mini internal loop** (maybe 5–10 feet of 3/8")

### 🔧 How to Try It:
- Pull the **bottom element or drain valve**
- Feed in a pre-coiled **mini-heat-exchange loop** (like a hand-wound 6–10" diameter)
- Use **bulkhead NPT adapters** to seal where the copper exits
- Fill tank back up with clean water → now you’ve got a **thermal battery with internal loop**

> This is trickier and only works if you have **enough clearance** through a port. Most element ports are 1" NPT = ~1.3" inner diameter.

---

## ✅ Option 3: Use the Tank as an External Loop Only

If you **can’t go inside or wrap** efficiently, turn the 50-gal tank into a **passive collector loop reservoir**:

- Run the **solar-heated water directly into the tank**
- Put a **copper coil INSIDE the 30-gal active tank** instead
- This flips the roles: the **main tank gets the exchanger**, the 50-gal is just the heated water source

---

That **old blue pressure tank** is a **perfect candidate** for hacking together a custom **solar thermal buffer tank with a built-in heat exchanger**. Since you're open to cutting it, you now have **full control over the internal structure**, and that unlocks all kinds of optimization.

---

## ✅ What Makes This Ideal
- **Steel shell**: good for holding heat, rugged
- **Already pressure-rated** (you don’t need pressure now, but it’s still tough)
- **Accessible ports**: likely has 3/4" or 1" NPT ports you can re-use
- **Freedom to insert, weld, bolt, or wrap whatever you want inside**

---

## 🧰 How to Convert the Blue Pressure Tank into a Thermal Battery

### Step 1: **Cut it open**
- Use an angle grinder or reciprocating saw
- Make a clean horizontal cut ~6–12” from the top so you can access the interior
- Save the top for welding/bolting back later or hinge it with clamps

---

### Step 2: **Insert a Copper Coil Heat Exchanger**
- Coil **25–50 ft of 1/2" or 3/8" soft copper tubing**
- Mount it low in the tank so it sits fully submerged when filled
- Anchor the coil with metal strapping or copper standoffs to prevent rattle
- Coil ends should pass through the tank wall via:
  - Existing ports (enlarge if needed)
  - Or **NPT bulkhead fittings**

**TIP:** You can also use **Pex-Al-Pex tubing** if you want flexibility with rigidity

---

### Step 3: **Add Fill + Drain + Temp Ports**
- Reuse the bottom port as a **fill/drain valve**
- Tap a 1/4" NPT port for a **temperature probe or thermowell**
- Optional: add a pressure relief valve for safety if you ever seal it

---

### Step 4: **Seal & Insulate**
- Weld the lid back on or use:
  - **Rubber gasket + hose clamps**
  - High-temp RTV sealant + mechanical clamping
- Wrap the tank in **R-10+ foam insulation**
- Add a **reflective barrier wrap** on the outside for thermal retention

---

### Final Flow

**Solar Loop:**
```plaintext
Pump → PEX box → copper coil inside tank → return
```

**House Water:**
```plaintext
Cold from well → through copper coil (inside blue tank) → into 30-gal heater
```

---

### 🔥 Bonus Ideas
- Add **PCM (Phase Change Material)** to absorb more heat (e.g. wax, salt packs)
- Install a **sight glass** to monitor water level
- If you're feeling spicy: mount it horizontally with **two coils** inside

---

| Feature               | Advantage                          |

| Full access interior   | Can install coil, PCM, sensors     |
| Tough steel shell      | High durability, long heat hold    |
| Existing NPT ports     | Easy plumbing interface            |

Exactly. You’re deep in the **DIY thermal engineering zone now** — and everything you're saying is spot-on:

---

## ✅ Core Understanding

> Yes: **The internal pressure is atmospheric**  
Because your solar loop is **closed and unpressurized** (or at most low-pressure with a small expansion tank), the thermal reservoir (whether it's the blue tank or filter housings) doesn’t need to be rated for house pressure.

You're **just moving fluid in a loop** through a collector, into a thermal mass, and back.

---

## 🧠 Your Ideas Are All Solid:

---

### 🔧 1. **Bank of Modified Filter Housings (Series Coils)**

**Pros:**
- Easy to source
- Already have NPT ports
- Stackable/modular (add or remove as needed)
- Can insert **small copper/stainless coils inside** for heat exchange
- Could double as PCM chambers if you get creative

**Cons:**
- Lower single-unit volume
- Need good insulation wrap
- Risk of plastic distortion at high temp (choose high-temp models)

> 🛠 If you have **4–6 large 10" housings**, you can run coils in each one and serially heat your working fluid, much like a multi-pass radiator.

---

### 🔧 2. **Double-line the Blue Pressure Tank + Foam Fill the Cavity**

This is an **awesome approach** if you want to convert the tank into a **thermos-style heat battery**.

#### Concept:
- Insert a slightly smaller steel or HDPE tank **inside** the blue pressure tank
- Leave a **1–2" air gap** all around
- Fill that gap with:
  - **Closed-cell spray foam**
  - Or **pourable two-part foam**
- Now you’ve created a **super-insulated thermal buffer**

**BONUS:**
- You can suspend the coil inside the inner liner
- Or make the **outer layer** your loop and the **inner tank** your water store

---

### 🔧 3. **Hybrid: Coil Between Tank Layers**
- Double-wall design:
  - Outer steel tank
  - Inner vessel (plastic or thin stainless)
  - **Copper coil spiral** sandwiched between them
- Pour foam after placing the coil — keeps it secure and submerged in thermal mass

---

### 🧱 Material Notes

| Material | Max Temp | Use Case |
|---------|----------|-----------|
| HDPE     | ~180°F   | Inner liner if not direct heat |
| CPVC     | ~200°F   | Piping sections |
| Copper   | ~400°F+  | Coils, direct solar fluid |
| Spray foam | ~180°F (closed-cell) | Thermal jacket |
| Mineral wool | ~1200°F | Fireproof wrap (optional outer layer) |

---

## 💡 Pro System Design Tip

Install:
- **Air vent** at the top of your loop (to purge bubbles)
- **Low-pressure expansion tank** on return line
- **Temp probe ports** on tank and loop exit
- **Drain valve** at the bottom of the tank loop

This gives you a **fully serviceable, closed solar heat battery system**.

---

I can give you:
- 🧰 A CAD-style schematic
- 📦 Parts list (with PEX, copper, foam, sensors)
- ⚙️ Pump + control logic (based on delta-T or smart timer)

Let me know your preferred size, tank type, and if you're heating water *only* or thinking *thermal air assist* later too.

---

##  Commercial Heat Exchanger Options You Can Buy Now

### 1. **Brazed Plate Solar Heat Exchangers**
High-efficiency compact units, ideal for transferring heat from the solar loop (glycol or water) to potable water.

- Offers **single- or double-walled designs**, UL-listed and glycol-compatible, suitable for domestic solar systems. citeturn0search0

### 3. **Integrated Copper Coil Tanks**
- Some off-the-shelf solar hot water tanks come with a **built-in copper coil heat exchanger** inside, specifically for mains-pressure systems or thermosiphon solar preheating. citeturn0search19turn0search17

Exactly — those **brazed plate heat exchangers** can be shockingly cheap for the performance they deliver.

---

## ✅ Short Answer:
- **Yes**, $40–60 models (like the **VEVOR 5"x12" 50-plate**) are often **plenty enough for 95% of home solar preheat systems**  
- **No**, you do **not** need multiples unless you're dealing with:
  - **Very high flow rates** (10+ GPM)
  - **Extremely low delta-T** (very small temp difference between sides)
  - **Redundant loops or zones** (e.g., you want to run radiant floor + domestic hot water)

---

## 🔍 How These Work

- They're made of thin stainless plates stacked like an accordion
- Your **solar-heated fluid** (e.g. glycol or water) flows through alternating plates
- Your **cold potable water** flows through the other plates in reverse direction (counterflow)
- The **thermal contact area is huge**, so they transfer heat extremely efficiently

---

## 🔥 Performance Snapshot (for a 40–50 plate model)

| Factor                  | Typical Capability                     |
|--------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Flow rate                | 2–8 GPM per side                        |
| Temp rise                | 30–50°F (depending on delta-T input)    |
| Power rating             | ~20–40 kW thermal equivalent (with good delta-T) |
| Materials                | 316L stainless, copper brazing          |

These exchangers are so efficient that **even small units can support**:
- Full household domestic hot water preheat
- Radiant floor loops
- Brewing applications

---

## 💡 Would Adding More Help?

| Scenario                        | Add More? | Why                                      |
|----------------------------------|-----------|-------------------------------------------|
| You want to heat faster           | ⚠️ Maybe   | Depends on your pump rate & delta-T       |
| You want redundancy               | ✅ Yes     | You can plumb in parallel or series       |
| You want different loop types     | ✅ Yes     | E.g., floor loop vs. water tank loop      |
| You’re running very cold fluid    | ✅ Maybe   | For low input temps, more surface area helps |
| You're using only one water tank  | ❌ No      | One high-efficiency unit is plenty        |

---

## 🧠 Pro Setup Tip

If you want **expandability**, you can:

- Start with **one 50-plate unit**
- Plumb in a **union fitting** or **quick-disconnect** nearby
- Later add a second exchanger in **parallel** or **series** if needed

---

### 🔥 1. **Can Glycol Be Made More Heat-Absorbing?**

Yes — but within **very specific limits**.

### 🧪 Base Glycol Mix:
- **Propylene glycol** (non-toxic) or **ethylene glycol** (toxic but more efficient)
- Mixed with distilled water — typical ratios:
  - **50/50**: freezes ~ -30°F, boils ~ 220°F
  - **60/40**: deeper freeze protection, slightly lower heat capacity

> 🔧 **Best ratio for solar thermal**: **40% glycol / 60% water**  
> This gives excellent freeze protection with **higher thermal capacity** (water absorbs more heat than glycol)

---

### ⚗️ Can Additives Improve Heat Absorption?

Yes — and here’s what’s real:

| Additive Type                 | Effect                                         | Notes |
|------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|-------|
| **Thermal stabilizers**       | Prevent degradation under high heat           | Found in solar-specific glycol brands |
| **Surfactants**               | Improve heat transfer at surface boundaries   | Some hydronic fluids include these |
| **Nanofluids (experimental)** | Dispersed metal oxides to increase conduction | Rare & expensive, mostly lab-level |
| **Dye (black)**               | Slight absorption boost in direct solar loops | Only useful if fluid is exposed to sun (not in PEX)

So in practice:
> The **best heat absorption** comes from tuning the **glycol-to-water ratio** — not exotic additives.

> **Go 40% glycol / 60% distilled water** for best thermal behavior in closed loops unless you're in deep freeze zones.

---

## ✅ What You're Building

> A DIY version of **pre-insulated thermal conduit**, just like what’s used in commercial radiant and solar installs — but cheaper and modular.

---

## 🧱 How to Do It Right

### Materials
- **3” PVC drain pipe** (solid wall, SDR-35 or Schedule 40)
- **Expanding foam** (low-expansion polyurethane preferred)
- **1/2" or 3/4" PEX** or copper inside
- Pipe caps or cleanout ends
- Spray silicone or sealant for edges

---

### 🛠️ Build Steps

1. **Drill 2 small entry/exit holes** in PVC caps (centered)
2. Run **PEX or copper** straight through the center of the pipe
3. **Center it** with temporary spacers or zip-tied crossbars (keep pipe from touching sides)
4. Fill pipe **partially with expanding foam** (do in stages — it expands a lot)
5. Let cure with caps **off or loosely fitted** so pressure doesn’t bulge the pipe
6. Once cured, **trim ends flush**, seal with silicone or screw-on cleanouts

---

## 🔥 Why This Works So Well

| Feature                         | Benefit                                 |
|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| **Foam core**                   | Insulates pipe — prevents heat loss     |
| **PVC jacket**                  | Waterproof, crush-resistant, durable     |
| **Centered PEX**                | Minimizes thermal bridging               |
| **Underground-safe**           | Can be buried shallow without freezing  |
| **Multiple runs**              | Use dual lines (supply/return) per conduit |
| **Modular**                     | Build in sections, link with couplers    |

> 💡 **This is essentially how commercial geothermal, radiant heat, and district solar lines are built.**

---

## 🧠 Pro Tips

- Use **low-expansion foam** or two-part pour foam to avoid deforming the PVC
- Label the ends (e.g., “SOLAR OUT / SOLAR RETURN”) to avoid confusion later
- If burying:
  - Grade slightly downhill toward the house
  - Run inside **4–6" corrugated drain pipe** as a sleeve if you want future removal access

---

## ✅ Summary

You just turned cheap PVC and a can of foam into a:
> 🔥 Fully insulated, underground-rated, protected, modular **solar thermal umbilical**.

And it looks clean. Runs stable. And eliminates 90% of the heat loss most DIY systems suffer from.

## ✅ 1. Use the **50-gal Tank’s Relief Valve** to Burp the System

You’re absolutely right — the **circulation pump can fill the system**, if plumbed with logic:

- Install a **fill tee on the intake side**

## ✅ 3. Create a **Vacuum Fill Port** (Brilliant Touch)

This is like automotive coolant fill kits — and very effective.

### 🛠 Setup:

```plaintext
    [Glycol Mix Bucket]
           ↓
     [Check Valve] ← one-way in
           ↓
     [Fill Valve or Tee]
           ↓
       [Pump Intake] ——→ System Loop
```

**How to Operate:**
1. Close all other outputs
2. Open fill valve
3. Run pump
4. Fluid gets sucked into system under vacuum
5. Burp air out the top (relief valve / vent tee)
6. Seal everything once loop is full

> You now have a **vacuum-assisted fill station** — no manual pressurization needed.

These are **precisely the kinds of questions** a system designer asks when stepping beyond function into **efficiency and control**. Let’s unpack each:

---

## ✅ 1. **How Big Do the Boxes (Solar Collectors) Need to Be?**

The “box” in this case is your **solar thermal collector area** — the thing absorbing sunlight to heat your glycol.

### 📐 Rule of Thumb:
For **solar hot water**, a good estimate is:

> **1.5 to 2 square feet of collector per gallon of daily hot water use**

But for your system — **preheating water into a 30-gal tank**, and given your light use except tub/shower — here’s a safe target:

| Daily Draw         | Collector Size (Minimum) |
|--------------------|--------------------------|
| 10–20 gal / day    | 15–25 sq ft               |
| 30–40 gal / day    | 25–35 sq ft               |

> 🎯 **Ideal for you**: ~24–30 square feet (2x 4'x4' panels or 1x 4'x8')

This could be:
- Black-painted PEX coils in a DIY glass/clear polycarbonate box
- Flat plate collectors (salvaged or purchased)
- Glazed aluminum panels
- DIY aluminum can panel (slow but fun project)

---

## ✅ 2. **PEX Line Size: 3/4" vs 1"**

### 🧠 Core Principles:

| Size    | Flow | Resistance | Best Use |
|---------|------|------------|-----------|
| **3/4"** | Moderate flow | ✅ Less heat loss, easy to work with | ✅ Ideal for most DIY loops |
| **1"**   | High flow | ✅ Lower pressure loss | Use only if you need >5 GPM over long distance |

> 🎯 **Your system is small/medium**, low-flow, heat retention > velocity.  
**Use 3/4" PEX** — it’s perfect. Less glycol, less pump strain, easier to insulate and route.

---

## ✅ 3. **Is It True That Black Heats Faster but Also Cools Faster?**

Yes — but with nuance. Here's the physics:

| Color      | Absorption (Sunlight) | Emission (Infrared) | Behavior |
|------------|------------------------|----------------------|----------|
| **Black**  | ✅ Absorbs nearly all incoming radiation | ✅ Radiates heat efficiently | Heats fast, **cools fast** |
| **White**  | ❌ Reflects most light | ❌ Radiates poorly    | Heats slowly, **cools slowly** |
| **Shiny (metal)** | ❌ Reflects light | ❌ Radiates very little | Stays coldest / holds heat |

> So yes:  
✔️ Black heats up faster under sunlight  
✔️ Black **also radiates** heat to its environment more quickly  
That’s **why** thermal collectors are **black AND insulated/glazed** — to trap that heat in.

---

## 🛠️ Apply This to Your Box Design

| Feature           | Recommendation |
|-------------------|----------------|
| **Interior color** | Flat black high-temp paint (max absorption) |
| **Cover**          | Clear polycarbonate or glass (greenhouse effect) |
| **Insulation**     | 1–2" rigid foam board on back and sides |
| **Absorber**       | Black PEX or black-painted aluminum fins |
| **Flow**           | Use logic to slow down when delta-T is low, and speed up when solar input peaks |

---

## ✅ Bonus: Smart Flow Logic

Control pump speed or on/off cycles based on:
- Solar temp probe vs tank temp probe
- Target delta-T (e.g., only run pump if solar is >10°F hotter than tank)
- Arduino/Pi PWM output for pump speed modulation

|------------------|----------------|
| Collector size   | ~24–30 sq ft   |
| PEX size         | 3/4"            |
| Box interior     | Flat black      |
| Insulation       | Back/sides w/ foam |
| Color physics    | Black = fast gain + fast loss → insulate and glaze it |
| Flow control     | Use sensors + Pi/Arduino logic for dynamic efficiency |

thoughts.content: Telerik docs confirm drag-and-drop is supported, and the service should handle events like PreviewDragDrop. The issue might be that the service is null if it's not created properly. Another possibility is that they haven't set `AllowDrag` correctly, but they haven’t gotten a null reference, so I'll look further into the drop target settings.

The `PreviewDragDrop` event uses `RadDropEventArgs`, which seems fine, but events still aren't firing. One possibility is that `radTaskBoard1.AllowDragDrop` isn't enabled. Another issue could be the drag happening between two task boards, which doesn't work unless it's within the same board. The column element might not be correctly attached.

It seems the issue is that task events aren’t firing because handlers aren’t subscribed. I need to suggest subscribing to `TaskCardAdding` and `TaskCardAdded` for columns. Also, dynamically adding columns means re-subscribing to events. I’ll provide code to hook those events and ensure no issues with suppressing drag functionality.

In this collection, Robert C. Martin, also known as “Uncle Bob,” provides a
pragmatic method for writing better code from the start. He reveals the
disciplines, techniques, tools, and practices that separate software craftsmen
from mere “9-to-5” programmers. Within this collection are the tools and
methods you need to become a true software professional.
To simplify access to each book, we’ve appended “A” to the pages of Clean
Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftmanship, and “B” to pages of
The Clean Coder: A Code of Conduct for Professional Programmers.This
enabled us to produce a single, comprehensive table of contents and
dedicated indexes.
We hope you find this collection useful!
—The editorial and production teams at Prentice Hall

For Ann Marie: The ever enduring love of my life.



Foreword

One of our favorite candies here in Denmark is Ga-Jol, whose strong
licorice vapors are a perfect complement to our damp and often chilly
weather. Part of the charm of Ga-Jol to us Danes is the wise or witty
sayings printed on the flap of every box top. I bought a two-pack of the
delicacy this morning and found that it bore this old Danish saw:

Ærlighed i små ting er ikke nogen lille ting.

“Honesty in small things is not a small thing.” It was a good omen
consistent with what I already wanted to say here. Small things matter. This
is a book about humble concerns whose value is nonetheless far from small.

God is in the details, said the architect Ludwig mies van der Rohe. This
quote recalls contemporary arguments about the role of architecture in
software development, and particularly in the Agile world. Bob and I
occasionally find ourselves passionately engaged in this dialogue. And yes,
mies van der Rohe was attentive to utility and to the timeless forms of
building that underlie great architecture. On the other hand, he also
personally selected every doorknob for every house he designed. Why?
Because small things matter.

In our ongoing “debate” on TDD, Bob and I have discovered that we agree
that software architecture has an important place in development, though
we likely have different visions of exactly what that means. Such quibbles
are relatively unimportant, however, because we can accept for granted that
responsible professionals give some time to thinking and planning at the
outset of a project. The late-1990s notions of design driven only by the tests
and the code are long gone. Yet attentiveness to detail is an even more
critical foundation of professionalism than is any grand vision. First, it is
through practice in the small that professionals gain proficiency and trust
for practice in the large. Second, the smallest bit of sloppy construction, of
the door that does not close tightly or the slightly crooked tile on the floor,
or even the messy desk, completely dispels the charm of the larger whole.
That is what clean code is about.



Still, architecture is just one metaphor for software development, and in
particular for that part of software that delivers the initial product in the
same sense that an architect delivers a pristine building. In these days of
Scrum and Agile, the focus is on quickly bringing product to market. We
want the factory running at top speed to produce software. These are human
factories: thinking, feeling coders who are working from a product backlog
or user story to create product. The manufacturing metaphor looms ever
strong in such thinking. The production aspects of Japanese auto
manufacturing, of an assembly-line world, inspire much of Scrum.

Yet even in the auto industry, the bulk of the work lies not in manufacturing
but in maintenance—or its avoidance. In software, 80% or more of what we
do is quaintly called “maintenance”: the act of repair. Rather than
embracing the typical Western focus on producing good software, we
should be thinking more like home repairmen in the building industry, or
auto mechanics in the automotive field. What does Japanese management
have to say about that?

In about 1951, a quality approach called Total Productive Maintenance
(TPM) came on the Japanese scene. Its focus is on maintenance rather than
on production. One of the major pillars of TPM is the set of so-called 5S
principles. 5S is a set of disciplines—and here I use the term “discipline”
instructively. These 5S principles are in fact at the foundations of Lean—
another buzzword on the Western scene, and an increasingly prominent
buzzword in software circles. These principles are not an option. As Uncle
Bob relates in his front matter, good software practice requires such
discipline: focus, presence of mind, and thinking. It is not always just about
doing, about pushing the factory equipment to produce at the optimal
velocity. The 5S philosophy comprises these concepts:

• Seiri, or organization (think “sort” in English). Knowing where things
are—using approaches such as suitable naming—is crucial. You think
naming identifiers isn’t important? Read on in the following chapters.

• Seiton, or tidiness (think “systematize” in English). There is an old
American saying: A place for everything, and everything in its place.
A piece of code should be where you expect to find it—and, if not, you
should re-factor to get it there.



• Seiso, or cleaning (think “shine” in English): Keep the workplace free
of hanging wires, grease, scraps, and waste. What do the authors here
say about littering your code with comments and commented-out code
lines that capture history or wishes for the future? Get rid of them.

• Seiketsu, or standardization: The group agrees about how to keep the
workplace clean. Do you think this book says anything about having a
consistent coding style and set of practices within the group? Where do
those standards come from? Read on.

• Shutsuke, or discipline (self-discipline). This means having the
discipline to follow the practices and to frequently reflect on one’s
work and be willing to change.

If you take up the challenge—yes, the challenge—of reading and applying
this book, you’ll come to understand and appreciate the last point. Here, we
are finally driving to the roots of responsible professionalism in a
profession that should be concerned with the life cycle of a product. As we
maintain automobiles and other machines under TPM, breakdown
maintenance—waiting for bugs to surface—is the exception. Instead, we go
up a level: inspect the machines every day and fix wearing parts before they
break, or do the equivalent of the proverbial 10,000-mile oil change to
forestall wear and tear. In code, refactor mercilessly. You can improve yet
one level further, as the TPM movement innovated over 50 years ago: build
machines that are more maintainable in the first place. Making your code
readable is as important as making it executable. The ultimate practice,
introduced in TPM circles around 1960, is to focus on introducing entire
new machines or replacing old ones. As Fred Brooks admonishes us, we
should probably re-do major software chunks from scratch every seven
years or so to sweep away creeping cruft. Perhaps we should update
Brooks’ time constant to an order of weeks, days or hours instead of years.
That’s where detail lies.

There is great power in detail, yet there is something humble and profound
about this approach to life, as we might stereotypically expect from any
approach that claims Japanese roots. But this is not only an Eastern outlook
on life; English and American folk wisdom are full of such admonishments.
The Seiton quote from above flowed from the pen of an Ohio minister who
literally viewed neatness “as a remedy for every degree of evil.” How about



Seiso? Cleanliness is next to godliness. As beautiful as a house is, a messy
desk robs it of its splendor. How about Shutsuke in these small matters? He
who is faithful in little is faithful in much. How about being eager to re-
factor at the responsible time, strengthening one’s position for subsequent
“big” decisions, rather than putting it off? A stitch in time saves nine. The
early bird catches the worm. Don’t put off until tomorrow what you can do
today. (Such was the original sense of the phrase “the last responsible
moment” in Lean until it fell into the hands of software consultants.) How
about calibrating the place of small, individual efforts in a grand whole?
Mighty oaks from little acorns grow. Or how about integrating simple
preventive work into everyday life? An ounce of prevention is worth a
pound of cure. An apple a day keeps the doctor away. Clean code honors
the deep roots of wisdom beneath our broader culture, or our culture as it
once was, or should be, and can be with attentiveness to detail.

Even in the grand architectural literature we find saws that hark back to
these supposed details. Think of mies van der Rohe’s doorknobs. That’s
seiri. That’s being attentive to every variable name. You should name a
variable using the same care with which you name a first-born child.

As every homeowner knows, such care and ongoing refinement never come
to an end. The architect Christopher Alexander—father of patterns and
pattern languages—views every act of design itself as a small, local act of
repair. And he views the craftsmanship of fine structure to be the sole
purview of the architect; the larger forms can be left to patterns and their
application by the inhabitants. Design is ever ongoing not only as we add a
new room to a house, but as we are attentive to repainting, replacing worn
carpets, or upgrading the kitchen sink. Most arts echo analogous sentiments.
In our search for others who ascribe God’s home as being in the details, we
find ourselves in the good company of the 19th century French author
Gustav Flaubert. The French poet Paul Valery advises us that a poem is
never done and bears continual rework, and to stop working on it is
abandonment. Such preoccupation with detail is common to all endeavors
of excellence. So maybe there is little new here, but in reading this book
you will be challenged to take up good disciplines that you long ago
surrendered to apathy or a desire for spontaneity and just “responding to
change.”



Unfortunately, we usually don’t view such concerns as key cornerstones of
the art of programming. We abandon our code early, not because it is done,
but because our value system focuses more on outward appearance than on
the substance of what we deliver. This inattentiveness costs us in the end: A
bad penny always shows up. Research, neither in industry nor in academia,
humbles itself to the lowly station of keeping code clean. Back in my days
working in the Bell Labs Software Production Research organization
(Production, indeed!) we had some back-of-the-envelope findings that
suggested that consistent indentation style was one of the most statistically
significant indicators of low bug density. We want it to be that architecture
or programming language or some other high notion should be the cause of
quality; as people whose supposed professionalism owes to the mastery of
tools and lofty design methods, we feel insulted by the value that those
factory-floor machines, the coders, add through the simple consistent
application of an indentation style. To quote my own book of 17 years ago,
such style distinguishes excellence from mere competence. The Japanese
worldview understands the crucial value of the everyday worker and, more
so, of the systems of development that owe to the simple, everyday actions
of those workers. Quality is the result of a million selfless acts of care—not
just of any great method that descends from the heavens. That these acts are
simple doesn’t mean that they are simplistic, and it hardly means that they
are easy. They are nonetheless the fabric of greatness and, more so, of
beauty, in any human endeavor. To ignore them is not yet to be fully human.

Of course, I am still an advocate of thinking at broader scope, and
particularly of the value of architectural approaches rooted in deep domain
knowledge and software usability. The book isn’t about that—or, at least, it
isn’t obviously about that. This book has a subtler message whose
profoundness should not be underappreciated. It fits with the current saw of
the really code-based people like Peter Sommerlad, Kevlin Henney and
Giovanni Asproni. “The code is the design” and “Simple code” are their
mantras. While we must take care to remember that the interface is the
program, and that its structures have much to say about our program
structure, it is crucial to continuously adopt the humble stance that the
design lives in the code. And while rework in the manufacturing metaphor
leads to cost, rework in design leads to value. We should view our code as
the beautiful articulation of noble efforts of design—design as a process,
not a static endpoint. It’s in the code that the architectural metrics of



coupling and cohesion play out. If you listen to Larry Constantine describe
coupling and cohesion, he speaks in terms of code—not lofty abstract
concepts that one might find in UML. Richard Gabriel advises us in his
essay, “Abstraction Descant” that abstraction is evil. Code is anti-evil, and
clean code is perhaps divine.

Going back to my little box of Ga-Jol, I think it’s important to note that the
Danish wisdom advises us not just to pay attention to small things, but also
to be honest in small things. This means being honest to the code, honest to
our colleagues about the state of our code and, most of all, being honest
with ourselves about our code. Did we Do our Best to “leave the
campground cleaner than we found it”? Did we re-factor our code before
checking in? These are not peripheral concerns but concerns that lie
squarely in the center of Agile values. It is a recommended practice in
Scrum that re-factoring be part of the concept of “Done.” Neither
architecture nor clean code insist on perfection, only on honesty and doing
the best we can. To err is human; to forgive, divine. In Scrum, we make
everything visible. We air our dirty laundry. We are honest about the state of
our code because code is never perfect. We become more fully human,
more worthy of the divine, and closer to that greatness in the details.

In our profession, we desperately need all the help we can get. If a clean
shop floor reduces accidents, and well-organized shop tools increase
productivity, then I’m all for them. As for this book, it is the best pragmatic
application of Lean principles to software I have ever seen in print. I
expected no less from this practical little group of thinking individuals that
has been striving together for years not only to become better, but also to
gift their knowledge to the industry in works such as you now find in your
hands. It leaves the world a little better than I found it before Uncle Bob
sent me the manuscript.

Having completed this exercise in lofty insights, I am off to clean my desk.

James O. Coplien
Mørdrup, Denmark



Introduction

Which door represents your code? Which door represents your team or your
company? Why are we in that room? Is this just a normal code review or
have we found a stream of horrible problems shortly after going live? Are
we debugging in a panic, poring over code that we thought worked? Are
customers leaving in droves and managers breathing down our necks? How
can we make sure we wind up behind the right door when the going gets
tough? The answer is: craftsmanship.

There are two parts to learning craftsmanship: knowledge and work. You
must gain the knowledge of principles, patterns, practices, and heuristics



that a craftsman knows, and you must also grind that knowledge into your
fingers, eyes, and gut by working hard and practicing.

I can teach you the physics of riding a bicycle. Indeed, the classical
mathematics is relatively straightforward. Gravity, friction, angular
momentum, center of mass, and so forth, can be demonstrated with less
than a page full of equations. Given those formulae I could prove to you
that bicycle riding is practical and give you all the knowledge you needed to
make it work. And you’d still fall down the first time you climbed on that
bike.

Coding is no different. We could write down all the “feel good” principles
of clean code and then trust you to do the work (in other words, let you fall
down when you get on the bike), but then what kind of teachers would that
make us, and what kind of student would that make you?

No. That’s not the way this book is going to work.

Learning to write clean code is hard work. It requires more than just the
knowledge of principles and patterns. You must sweat over it. You must
practice it yourself, and watch yourself fail. You must watch others practice
it and fail. You must see them stumble and retrace their steps. You must see
them agonize over decisions and see the price they pay for making those
decisions the wrong way.

Be prepared to work hard while reading this book. This is not a “feel good”
book that you can read on an airplane and finish before you land. This book
will make you work, and work hard. What kind of work will you be doing?
You’ll be reading code—lots of code. And you will be challenged to think
about what’s right about that code and what’s wrong with it. You’ll be asked
to follow along as we take modules apart and put them back together again.
This will take time and effort; but we think it will be worth it.

We have divided this book into three parts. The first several chapters
describe the principles, patterns, and practices of writing clean code. There
is quite a bit of code in these chapters, and they will be challenging to read.
They’ll prepare you for the second section to come. If you put the book
down after reading the first section, good luck to you!

The second part of the book is the harder work. It consists of several case
studies of ever-increasing complexity. Each case study is an exercise in



cleaning up some code—of transforming code that has some problems into
code that has fewer problems. The detail in this section is intense. You will
have to flip back and forth between the narrative and the code listings. You
will have to analyze and understand the code we are working with and walk
through our reasoning for making each change we make. Set aside some
time because this should take you days.

The third part of this book is the payoff. It is a single chapter containing a
list of heuristics and smells gathered while creating the case studies. As we
walked through and cleaned up the code in the case studies, we documented
every reason for our actions as a heuristic or smell. We tried to understand
our own reactions to the code we were reading and changing, and worked
hard to capture why we felt what we felt and did what we did. The result is
a knowledge base that desribes the way we think when we write, read, and
clean code.

This knowledge base is of limited value if you don’t do the work of
carefully reading through the case studies in the second part of this book. In
those case studies we have carefully annotated each change we made with
forward references to the heuristics. These forward references appear in
square brackets like this: [H22]. This lets you see the context in which those
heuristics were applied and written! It is not the heuristics themselves that
are so valuable, it is the relationship between those heuristics and the
discrete decisions we made while cleaning up the code in the case studies.

To further help you with those relationships, we have placed a cross-
reference at the end of the book that shows the page number for every
forward reference. You can use it to look up each place where a certain
heuristic was applied.

If you read the first and third sections and skip over the case studies, then
you will have read yet another “feel good” book about writing good
software. But if you take the time to work through the case studies,
following every tiny step, every minute decision—if you put yourself in our
place, and force yourself to think along the same paths that we thought, then
you will gain a much richer understanding of those principles, patterns,
practices, and heuristics. They won’t be “feel good” knowledge any more.
They’ll have been ground into your gut, fingers, and heart. They’ll have



become part of you in the same way that a bicycle becomes an extension of
your will when you have mastered how to ride it.

On the Cover

The image on the cover is M104: The Sombrero Galaxy. M104 is located in
Virgo and is just under 30 million light-years from us. At it’s core is a
supermassive black hole weighing in at about a billion solar masses.

Does the image remind you of the explosion of the Klingon power moon
Praxis? I vividly remember the scene in Star Trek VI that showed an
equatorial ring of debris flying away from that explosion. Since that scene,
the equatorial ring has been a common artifact in sci-fi movie explosions. It
was even added to the explosion of Alderaan in later editions of the first
Star Wars movie.

What caused this ring to form around M104? Why does it have such a huge
central bulge and such a bright and tiny nucleus? It looks to me as though
the central black hole lost its cool and blew a 30,000 light-year hole in the
middle of the galaxy. Woe befell any civilizations that might have been in
the path of that cosmic disruption.

Supermassive black holes swallow whole stars for lunch, converting a
sizeable fraction of their mass to energy. E = MC2 is leverage enough, but
when M is a stellar mass: Look out! How many stars fell headlong into that
maw before the monster was satiated? Could the size of the central void be
a hint?

The image of M104 on the cover is a combination of the famous visible
light photograph from Hubble (right), and the recent infrared image from
the Spitzer orbiting observatory (below, right). It’s the infrared image that
clearly shows us the ring nature of the galaxy. In visible light we only see
the front edge of the ring in silhouette. The central bulge obscures the rest
of the ring.

But in the infrared, the hot particles in the ring shine through the central
bulge. The two images combined give us a view we’ve not seen before and
imply that long ago it was a raging inferno of activity.
